claim: Between fiscal years 1998 and 2021, NIH issued 827,815 RPG awards of at least $25,000 per year (BRDPI-indexed to FY2021).
source: Between FY1998 and FY2021, NIH issued 827,815 RPG awards of at least $25,000 per year (BRDPI-indexed to FY2021).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific numerical data from NIH IMPAC II files about the number of RPG awards issued during the specified time period.

claim: The number of RPGs and Principal Investigators supported on RPGs increased during the NIH budget doubling from FY1998 to FY2003.
source: The number of RPGs and Principal Investigators supported on RPGs increased during the NIH budget doubling (from FY1998 to FY2003), decreased gradually between the end of the doubling and FY2015, and increased again with recent NIH budget increases (Figure 1, panel A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1, panel A, which shows trends in RPG awards and Principal Investigators over time.

claim: The number of RPGs and Principal Investigators decreased gradually between the end of the doubling and FY2015.
source: The number of RPGs and Principal Investigators supported on RPGs increased during the NIH budget doubling (from FY1998 to FY2003), decreased gradually between the end of the doubling and FY2015, and increased again with recent NIH budget increases (Figure 1, panel A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1, panel A, showing the trend after the budget doubling period.

claim: The number of RPGs and Principal Investigators increased again with recent NIH budget increases after FY2015.
source: The number of RPGs and Principal Investigators supported on RPGs increased during the NIH budget doubling (from FY1998 to FY2003), decreased gradually between the end of the doubling and FY2015, and increased again with recent NIH budget increases (Figure 1, panel A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 1, panel A, showing recent trends in RPG awards.

claim: Between FY1998 and FY2012, the BRDPI was consistently higher than the GDP Price Index.
source: Between FY1998 and FY2012 the BRDPI was consistently higher than the GDP Price Index (NIH, 2022c); after FY2012, when the government imposed lower caps on compensation of extramural investigators, the BRDPI has fallen to the same levels as the GDP Price Index (Figure 1, panel B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from NIH Office of the Budget and visualized in Figure 1, panel B.

claim: After FY2012, when the government imposed lower caps on compensation of extramural investigators, the BRDPI has fallen to the same levels as the GDP Price Index.
source: Between FY1998 and FY2012 the BRDPI was consistently higher than the GDP Price Index (NIH, 2022c); after FY2012, when the government imposed lower caps on compensation of extramural investigators, the BRDPI has fallen to the same levels as the GDP Price Index (Figure 1, panel B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from NIH Office of the Budget and visualized in Figure 1, panel B, with an inference about the causal relationship to salary caps.

claim: Both the BRDPI and the GDP Price Index are projected to increase in FY2022, but decrease to close to FY2021 levels over the next 2 years.
source: Both the BRDPI and the GDP Price Index are projected to increase in FY2022, but decrease to close to FY2021 levels over the next 2 years; these projections should be interpreted with caution given recent price volatility linked to the COVID-19 pandemic and supply-chain interruptions (Figure 1, panel B) (NIH, 2022c).
evidence: The claim is based on projected data from NIH Office of the Budget, shown in Figure 1, panel B.

claim: Mean and median real (FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted) total costs of RPGs increased during the doubling of FY1998-FY2003 from average values of about $530,000 to about $610,000.
source: Mean and median real (that is FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted) total costs of RPGs increased during the doubling of FY1998-FY2003 (from average values of about $530,000 to about $610,000), fell to a nadir of about $520,000 in FY2013 (the year of budget sequestration), and after a quick rebound in FY2014 has remained relatively stable at about $570,000 since (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 2 showing trends in RPG costs.

claim: Mean and median real total costs of RPGs fell to a nadir of about $520,000 in FY2013 (the year of budget sequestration).
source: Mean and median real (that is FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted) total costs of RPGs increased during the doubling of FY1998-FY2003 (from average values of about $530,000 to about $610,000), fell to a nadir of about $520,000 in FY2013 (the year of budget sequestration), and after a quick rebound in FY2014 has remained relatively stable at about $570,000 since (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 2 showing the lowest point in RPG costs.

claim: After a quick rebound in FY2014, mean and median real total costs of RPGs have remained relatively stable at about $570,000.
source: Mean and median real (that is FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted) total costs of RPGs increased during the doubling of FY1998-FY2003 (from average values of about $530,000 to about $610,000), fell to a nadir of about $520,000 in FY2013 (the year of budget sequestration), and after a quick rebound in FY2014 has remained relatively stable at about $570,000 since (Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data analysis presented in Figure 2 showing recent stability in RPG costs.

claim: Similar trends in real costs were seen with real indirect costs of RPGs.
source: Similar trends were seen with real indirect costs of RPGs, which if anything have increased modestly in more recent year (Figure 3) and for total real costs of R01-equivalent awards (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing trends in indirect costs.

claim: Real indirect costs of RPGs have increased modestly in more recent years.
source: Similar trends were seen with real indirect costs of RPGs, which if anything have increased modestly in more recent year (Figure 3) and for total real costs of R01-equivalent awards (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 3 showing a modest increase in indirect costs.

claim: Similar trends in real costs were seen for total real costs of R01-equivalent awards.
source: Similar trends were seen with real indirect costs of RPGs, which if anything have increased modestly in more recent year (Figure 3) and for total real costs of R01-equivalent awards (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 4 showing trends in R01-equivalent award costs.

claim: Over time there have been decreases in the proportion of unsolicited awards.
source: Over time there have been decreases in the proportion of unsolicited awards and program ('P') grants, while there have been increases in the proportions of R21 or R03 grants, cooperative agreements, clinical trials (since reliable data were first collected in FY2008), highly expensive projects (defined as those costing at least $5 million in FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted, that is real, values), and human-studies only projects (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing changes in award characteristics over time.

claim: Over time there have been decreases in the proportion of program ('P') grants.
source: Over time there have been decreases in the proportion of unsolicited awards and program ('P') grants, while there have been increases in the proportions of R21 or R03 grants, cooperative agreements, clinical trials (since reliable data were first collected in FY2008), highly expensive projects (defined as those costing at least $5 million in FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted, that is real, values), and human-studies only projects (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing changes in award characteristics over time.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing changes in award characteristics over time.

claim: Over time there have been increases in the proportions of clinical trials since reliable data were first collected in FY2008.
source: Over time there have been decreases in the proportion of unsolicited awards and program ('P') grants, while there have been increases in the proportions of R21 or R03 grants, cooperative agreements, clinical trials (since reliable data were first collected in FY2008), highly expensive projects (defined as those costing at least $5 million in FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted, that is real, values), and human-studies only projects (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing changes in award characteristics over time, with a note about data availability.

claim: Over time there have been increases in the proportions of highly expensive projects (defined as those costing at least $5 million in FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted values).
source: Over time there have been decreases in the proportion of unsolicited awards and program ('P') grants, while there have been increases in the proportions of R21 or R03 grants, cooperative agreements, clinical trials (since reliable data were first collected in FY2008), highly expensive projects (defined as those costing at least $5 million in FY2021 BRDPI-adjusted, that is real, values), and human-studies only projects (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing changes in award characteristics over time.

evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Table 1 showing changes in award characteristics over time.

claim: The proportion of R01-equivalent awards increased during the doubling and then returned to FY1998 levels.
source: The proportion of R01-equivalent awards increased during the doubling and then returned to FY1998 levels.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of data presented in Table 1 showing changes in R01-equivalent award proportions.

claim: Institutes of higher education, independent research organizations, and independent hospitals have consistently accounted for over 97 percent of awards.
source: Institutes of higher education, independent research organizations, and independent hospitals have consistently accounted for over 97 percent of awards.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of organization type data presented in Table 1.

claim: Among R01-equivalent awards, the proportion of awards with nominal direct costs less than $250,000 has decreased over time.
source: Among R01-equivalent awards, the proportion of awards with nominal direct costs less than $250,000 has decreased over time, while the proportion of awards with nominal direct costs greater than $500,000 has increased.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of data presented in Table 2 showing changes in direct cost distributions.

claim: Among R01-equivalent awards, the proportion of awards with nominal direct costs greater than $500,000 has increased over time.
source: Among R01-equivalent awards, the proportion of awards with nominal direct costs less than $250,000 has decreased over time, while the proportion of awards with nominal direct costs greater than $500,000 has increased.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of data presented in Table 2 showing changes in direct cost distributions.

claim: The $250,000 and $500,000 thresholds correspond to cut-offs for submission of simplified modular budgets and for required pre-approval for application.
source: These values correspond to cut-offs for submission of simplified modular budgets and for required pre-approval for application (Table 2).
evidence: The claim draws on established NIH policy knowledge about budget submission requirements.

claim: From the time of the doubling until about FY2010, the whisker range (distance between whisker tips in box plots) decreased.
source: From the time of the doubling until about FY2010, the distance between the whisker tips decreased. We call this distance the 'whisker range'. From FY2012 through FY2021 whisker ranges increased, exceeding levels for the doubling for untransformed costs, and not quite reaching doubling levels for log-transformed costs.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of box plot distributions shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: From FY2012 through FY2021, whisker ranges increased, exceeding levels for the doubling for untransformed costs.
source: From the time of the doubling until about FY2010, the distance between the whisker tips decreased. We call this distance the 'whisker range'. From FY2012 through FY2021 whisker ranges increased, exceeding levels for the doubling for untransformed costs, and not quite reaching doubling levels for log-transformed costs.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of box plot distributions shown in Appendix 1—figure 2.

claim: Whisker ranges declined from $920,000 to $750,000 between FY2002 and FY2010.
source: Figure 5 shows the whisker ranges declined from $920,000 to $750,000 between FY2002 and FY2010 and increased to over $1 million in FY2021 (panel A, with log-transformed values shown in panel B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5 showing changes in whisker ranges over time.

claim: Whisker ranges increased to over $1 million in FY2021.
source: Figure 5 shows the whisker ranges declined from $920,000 to $750,000 between FY2002 and FY2010 and increased to over $1 million in FY2021 (panel A, with log-transformed values shown in panel B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data presented in Figure 5 showing changes in whisker ranges over time.

claim: In FY1998, the top centile of RPG awards received 8% of funding.
source: In FY1998, the top centile of RPG awards received 8% of funding, rising to 12% FY2017; this 4% absolute difference means that an additional $850 million were awarded to approximately 350 grants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of funding distribution data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: By FY2017, the top centile of RPG awards received 12% of funding.
source: In FY1998, the top centile of RPG awards received 8% of funding, rising to 12% FY2017; this 4% absolute difference means that an additional $850 million were awarded to approximately 350 grants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of funding distribution data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The 4% absolute difference in funding to the top centile means that an additional $850 million were awarded to approximately 350 grants.
source: In FY1998, the top centile of RPG awards received 8% of funding, rising to 12% FY2017; this 4% absolute difference means that an additional $850 million were awarded to approximately 350 grants.
evidence: The claim is based on calculation from funding distribution data.

claim: There was little change in the proportion of funding going to the top decile of RPG awards.
source: There was little change in the proportion of funding going to the top decile; thus the upper extreme seems to be driven by increases in funding going to the most expensive awards (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of funding distribution data shown in Appendix 1—figure 3.

claim: The upper extreme in funding distribution seems to be driven by increases in funding going to the most expensive awards.
source: There was little change in the proportion of funding going to the top decile; thus the upper extreme seems to be driven by increases in funding going to the most expensive awards (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the analysis of funding distribution patterns.

claim: Before FY2010, unsolicited RPGs had a central tendency towards greater costs.
source: Before FY2010 unsolicited RPGs had a central tendency towards greater costs, but since then solicited awards were more costly (Figure 6, panel A).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of cost distributions by solicitation status shown in Figure 6, panel A.

claim: Since FY2010, solicited awards were more costly than unsolicited awards.
source: Before FY2010 unsolicited RPGs had a central tendency towards greater costs, but since then solicited awards were more costly (Figure 6, panel A).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of cost distributions by solicitation status shown in Figure 6, panel A.

claim: The proportion of solicited projects increased from 20% to 30% from FY1998 to FY2005.
source: The proportion of solicited projects increased from 20% to 30% from FY1998 to FY2005, then remained stable until FY2016, and increased to 40% from FY2016 to FY2021.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of solicitation trends shown in Figure 6, panel B.

claim: The proportion of solicited projects remained stable from FY2005 until FY2016.
source: The proportion of solicited projects increased from 20% to 30% from FY1998 to FY2005, then remained stable until FY2016, and increased to 40% from FY2016 to FY2021.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of solicitation trends shown in Figure 6, panel B.

claim: The proportion of solicited projects increased to 40% from FY2016 to FY2021.
source: The proportion of solicited projects increased from 20% to 30% from FY1998 to FY2005, then remained stable until FY2016, and increased to 40% from FY2016 to FY2021.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of solicitation trends shown in Figure 6, panel B.

claim: The proportion of funds going to solicited projects has steadily increased from 20% in FY1998 to 50% in FY2021.
source: Meanwhile the proportion of funds going to solicited projects has steadily increased from 20% in FY1998 to 50% in FY2021 (Figure 6, panel B).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of funding allocation trends shown in Figure 6, panel B.

claim: Throughout time, solicited projects have much greater degrees of variation in costs as reflected in larger whisker ranges.
source: Box-plot distributions over time of log-transformed costs of unsolicited (Appendix 1—figure 4, panel A) and solicited (Appendix 1—figure 4, panel B) projects show variations in whisker ranges (Figures 7 and 8), but throughout time solicited projects have much greater degrees of variation as reflected in larger whisker ranges (Figure 8); in more recent years the whisker ranges for solicited projected, while still much higher than for unsolicited projects, have decreased (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of box plot distributions shown in Figures 7 and 8.

claim: In more recent years, the whisker ranges for solicited projects, while still much higher than for unsolicited projects, have decreased.
source: Box-plot distributions over time of log-transformed costs of unsolicited (Appendix 1—figure 4, panel A) and solicited (Appendix 1—figure 4, panel B) projects show variations in whisker ranges (Figures 7 and 8), but throughout time solicited projects have much greater degrees of variation as reflected in larger whisker ranges (Figure 8); in more recent years the whisker ranges for solicited projected, while still much higher than for unsolicited projects, have decreased (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of box plot distributions shown in Figure 8.

claim: In FY2021, solicited projects were more expensive than unsolicited projects (mean of $710,000 versus $480,000).
source: In FY2021 solicited projects were more expensive (mean of $710,000 versus $480,000), and more likely to be over $5 million, to be a cooperative agreement, to be a clinical trial, and to involve human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: In FY2021, solicited projects were more likely to be over $5 million than unsolicited projects.
source: In FY2021 solicited projects were more expensive (mean of $710,000 versus $480,000), and more likely to be over $5 million, to be a cooperative agreement, to be a clinical trial, and to involve human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: In FY2021, solicited projects were more likely to be a cooperative agreement than unsolicited projects.
source: In FY2021 solicited projects were more expensive (mean of $710,000 versus $480,000), and more likely to be over $5 million, to be a cooperative agreement, to be a clinical trial, and to involve human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: In FY2021, solicited projects were more likely to be a clinical trial than unsolicited projects.
source: In FY2021 solicited projects were more expensive (mean of $710,000 versus $480,000), and more likely to be over $5 million, to be a cooperative agreement, to be a clinical trial, and to involve human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: In FY2021, solicited projects were more likely to involve human participants than unsolicited projects.
source: In FY2021 solicited projects were more expensive (mean of $710,000 versus $480,000), and more likely to be over $5 million, to be a cooperative agreement, to be a clinical trial, and to involve human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: Solicited projects were more likely to be funded through small R21 or R03 mechanisms.
source: Solicited projects were also more likely to be funded through small R21 or R03 mechanisms, while much less likely to be funded via an R01-equivalent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: Solicited projects were much less likely to be funded via an R01-equivalent mechanism.
source: Solicited projects were also more likely to be funded through small R21 or R03 mechanisms, while much less likely to be funded via an R01-equivalent mechanism.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 3.

claim: The wide whisker ranges of solicited projects may reflect both expensive and inexpensive awards.
source: Thus, the wide whisker ranges of solicited projects (Figure 8), which have become more common over time (Figure 6, panel B), may reflect both expensive and inexpensive awards.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the analysis of cost distributions and award types.

claim: Inexpensive R21 and R03 awards have increased from 5% of projects in FY1998 to nearly 16% in FY2015.
source: Inexpensive R21 and R03 awards have increased from 5% of projects in FY1998 to nearly 16% in FY2015, with a modest decline since (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of award mechanism trends shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: R21 and R03 awards have shown a modest decline since FY2015.
source: Inexpensive R21 and R03 awards have increased from 5% of projects in FY1998 to nearly 16% in FY2015, with a modest decline since (Appendix 1—figure 5).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of award mechanism trends shown in Appendix 1—figure 5.

claim: In FY2021, solicited R01-equivalent awards were more expensive than unsolicited R01-equivalent awards.
source: Solicited R01-equivalent awards were more expensive and more likely to involve clinical trials and human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 4.

claim: In FY2021, solicited R01-equivalent awards were more likely to involve clinical trials than unsolicited R01-equivalent awards.
source: Solicited R01-equivalent awards were more expensive and more likely to involve clinical trials and human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 4.

claim: In FY2021, solicited R01-equivalent awards were more likely to involve human participants than unsolicited R01-equivalent awards.
source: Solicited R01-equivalent awards were more expensive and more likely to involve clinical trials and human participants.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 4.

claim: Solicited R01-equivalent awards were less likely to have nominal direct costs less than $250,000.
source: Consistent with higher costs, they were less likely to have nominal direct costs less than $250,000 and more likely to have nominal direct costs greater than $500,000.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 4.

claim: Solicited R01-equivalent awards were more likely to have nominal direct costs greater than $500,000.
source: Consistent with higher costs, they were less likely to have nominal direct costs less than $250,000 and more likely to have nominal direct costs greater than $500,000.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of FY2021 data presented in Table 4.

claim: RPGs involving clinical trials are more expensive than other RPGs.
source: RPGs involving clinical trials are more expensive but, at least, over the last 10 years real costs remain stable (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of clinical trial costs shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Over the last 10 years, real costs of RPGs involving clinical trials remain stable.
source: RPGs involving clinical trials are more expensive but, at least, over the last 10 years real costs remain stable (Appendix 1—figure 6).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of clinical trial costs shown in Appendix 1—figure 6.

claim: Real-cost trends among RPGs are similar irrespective of human or animal classification.
source: Real-cost trends among RPGs are similar irrespective of human or animal classification, though as expected projects involving human participants or human participants and animal models were more expensive than others (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of costs by study type shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Projects involving human participants or human participants and animal models were more expensive than others.
source: Real-cost trends among RPGs are similar irrespective of human or animal classification, though as expected projects involving human participants or human participants and animal models were more expensive than others (Appendix 1—figure 7).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of costs by study type shown in Appendix 1—figure 7.

claim: Multivariable linear regressions with log-10 transformed costs as the dependent variable showed poor model fit due to fat-tailed distributions.
source: We attempted multivariable linear regressions with log-10 transformed costs as the dependent variable (Appendix 1—table 1; Leifeld, 2013), but upon inspection of residual diagnostics found poor model fit due to fat-tailed distributions.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis results and diagnostic evaluation.

claim: Other possible transformations (e.g. arcsinh, Box-Cox, center and scale, exponential, square-root, and Yeo-Johnson) did not result in substantive improvements in model fit.
source: We looked into other possible transformations (e.g. arcsinh, Box-Cox, center and scale, exponential, square-root, and Yeo-Johnson) and did not find substantive improvements.
evidence: The claim is based on exploratory analysis of different transformation methods.

claim: The random forest regression model, based on a one-percent random sample, was able to explain over 47% of the variance of costs.
source: The model, based on a one-percent random sample, performed well, able to explain over 47% of the variance of costs.
evidence: The claim is based on the performance metrics of the random forest model.

claim: Time (fiscal year) contributed little to prediction in the random forest model.
source: Time (that is fiscal year) contributed little to prediction (Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on variable importance analysis from the random forest model shown in Appendix 1—table 2.

claim: After adjusting for confounders, there is no independent association of time with BRDPI-adjusted costs.
source: After adjusting for potential confounders in a wholly non-parametric machine learning regression, we find no independent association of time with BRDPI-adjusted costs.
evidence: The claim is based on the results of the random forest regression analysis.

claim: Changes in real costs are largely explained by changes in the composition of the NIH-grant portfolio.
source: Recalling the automobile rental firm analogy, NIH may be pursuing the strategy of simultaneously purchasing more expensive (large vans) and less expensive (compact cars) vehicles, reflective of changing priorities and compositional effects over time.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the regression analysis and descriptive findings about portfolio composition.

claim: The rate of inflation for NIH-funded research (the BRDPI) was higher than the general rate of inflation from FY1998 until FY2012.
source: The rate of inflation for NIH-funded research (that is the BRDPI) was higher than the general rate of inflation from FY1998 until FY2012; since then, the rate of inflation for NIH-funded research has been similar to the general rate of inflation.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of BRDPI and general inflation data.

claim: Since FY2012, the rate of inflation for NIH-funded research has been similar to the general rate of inflation.
source: The rate of inflation for NIH-funded research (that is the BRDPI) was higher than the general rate of inflation from FY1998 until FY2012; since then, the rate of inflation for NIH-funded research has been similar to the general rate of inflation.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of BRDPI and general inflation data.

claim: Since 2005, the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) uses a Fisher chain-weighted indexed methodology for determining the BRDPI.
source: The BRDPI is determined via a sophisticated methodology; since 2005 the Bureau of Economic Analysis (BEA) uses a Fisher chain-weighted indexed methodology which is analogous to calculating compound growth on retirement portfolios over many years as the mix of stocks and bonds changes from year to year.
evidence: The claim describes the established methodology used by BEA for calculating the BRDPI.

claim: The decrease in the BRDPI in FY2012 was likely related to an NIH-imposed salary cap 'freeze' in 2011.
source: The decrease in the BRDPI in FY2012 was likely related to an NIH-imposed salary cap 'freeze' in 2011.
evidence: The claim is an inference about the causal relationship between salary cap policy and BRDPI changes.

claim: In 2012, the NIH linked the salary cap to Executive Level II (instead of the higher Executive Level I) salaries.
source: In 2012, the NIH has linked the salary cap to Executive Level II (instead of the higher Executive Level I) salaries.
evidence: The claim describes a specific NIH policy change.

claim: Since 2012, salary caps continue to be linked to Executive Level II levels and have increased at the rate of Federal civilian salaries.
source: Since then, salary caps continue to linked to Executive Level II levels and have increased at the rate of Federal civilian salaries, which likely have risen a rate lower than academic salaries.
evidence: The claim describes ongoing NIH salary cap policy.

claim: Federal civilian salaries have likely risen at a rate lower than academic salaries.
source: Since then, salary caps continue to linked to Executive Level II levels and have increased at the rate of Federal civilian salaries, which likely have risen a rate lower than academic salaries.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the relative rates of salary increases.

claim: The cap reductions in FY2011, the relatively slow rate of rise of Federal salaries, and relatively low increases in fellowship and training stipends have combined to reduce the BRDPI since FY2011.
source: The cap reductions in FY2011, the relatively slow rate of rise of Federal salaries which determine the NIH salary cap, along with relatively low increases in fellowship and training stipends have combined to reduce the BRDPI since FY2011 (NIH, 2022c).
evidence: The claim is an inference about the combined effects of multiple policy factors on the BRDPI, supported by NIH data.

claim: Institutions and faculty may be under greater pressures as the differential between NIH-imposed salary caps and actual faculty salaries increases.
source: Institutions and faculty may be under greater pressures as the differential between NIH-imposed salary caps and actual faculty salaries increases (NIH, 2022c).
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the consequences of the salary cap differential, referencing NIH data.

claim: Institutions and faculty are facing pressures due to increasing competition for post-doctoral research fellows who realize greater shorter and longer term economic success outside of the academy.
source: They are also facing pressures due to increasing competition for post-doctoral research fellows who realize greater shorter and longer term economic success outside of the academy (Kahn and Ginther, 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to research on postdoctoral career outcomes.

claim: Real (BRDPI-adjusted) average and median RPG costs increased during the NIH-doubling (FY1998 to FY2003).
source: Real (BRDPI-adjusted) average and median RPG costs increased during the NIH-doubling (FY1998 to FY2003), decreased after the doubling and have remained relatively stable since.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Real average and median RPG costs decreased after the doubling.
source: Real (BRDPI-adjusted) average and median RPG costs increased during the NIH-doubling (FY1998 to FY2003), decreased after the doubling and have remained relatively stable since.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Real average and median RPG costs have remained relatively stable since the post-doubling decrease.
source: Real (BRDPI-adjusted) average and median RPG costs increased during the NIH-doubling (FY1998 to FY2003), decreased after the doubling and have remained relatively stable since.
evidence: The claim summarizes findings from the data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The degree of variation of RPG costs has changed over time, with more marked extremes observed on both higher and lower levels of cost.
source: Of note, though, the degree of variation of RPG costs has changed over time, with more marked extremes observed on both higher and lower levels of cost.

claim: Inflation is defined by the United States Federal Reserve as 'the increase in the prices of goods and services over time'.

claim: Inflation has been a longstanding concern in the biomedical research community.
source: Inflation, defined by the United States Federal Reserve as 'the increase in the prices of goods and services over time' (US Federal Reserve, 2022), has been a longstanding concern in the biomedical research community. (Mervis, 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to literature on biomedical research concerns.

claim: Research Project Grants (RPGs) account for over half of the NIH budget.
source: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) issues different type of research and training awards, but by far the most common type is the "Research Project Grant (RPG)"(NIH, 2022a) accounting for over half of the NIH budget. (NIH, 2022b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to NIH budget information.

claim: Increases in costs for research may be greater than increases in general economy-wide costs just as educational and health-care costs have increased at rates much greater than other costs.
source: Increases in costs for research may be greater than increases in general economy-wide costs just as educational and health-care costs have increased at rates much greater than other costs.
evidence: The claim draws on established knowledge about differential inflation rates in service sectors.

claim: William Baumol explored differential increases in costs in his work on 'the cost disease'.
source: The Nobel-prize winning economist William Baumol explored differential increases in costs in his work on 'the cost disease'. (Malach and Baumol, 2012)
evidence: The claim cites Baumol's economic theory about cost increases in service sectors.

claim: The fundamental problem in Baumol's cost disease is that different sectors of the economy realize different rates of improvements in productivity.
source: The fundamental problem is that different sectors of the economy realize different rates of improvements in productivity.
evidence: The claim explains the core concept of Baumol's cost disease theory.

claim: It takes the same number of musicians the same amount of time to produce a live performance of a Beethoven string quartet now as it did in 1826.
source: Baumol cites 4 musicians who play a Beethoven string quartet; there has been no change in productivity between 1826 and now. It takes just as many musicians just as much time to 'produce' a live performance of a Beethoven string quartet.
evidence: The claim uses Baumol's classic example to illustrate the concept of stagnant productivity in certain sectors.

claim: The NIH caps on salaries and salary increases since 2012 may well have mitigated the effects of the cost disease on the NIH portfolio.
source: It is important to note, though, that the NIH caps on salaries and salary increases since 2012 may well have mitigated the effects of the cost disease on the NIH portfolio.
evidence: The claim is a speculation about the impact of NIH salary cap policies on cost trends.

claim: Bureau of Economic Analysis data on the relative costs of goods and services in the United States since 1950 show that the United States economy has shifted from goods to services.

claim: The relative prices for services (like education and healthcare) have increased since 1950.

evidence: The claim cites economic data about price trends in service sectors.
